name: Cunningham C-4R
hook: At Le Mans in 1952, Briggs Cunningham drove his own car for almost twenty of the twenty-four hours and finished fourth.
story: Briggs Cunningham wanted to win Le Mans in an American car with his own name on it. There was a catch. To enter under your own badge, you had to be a car maker. So he became one. His shop in West Palm Beach built a road car called the C-3. The chassis were shipped to Vignale in Turin for elegant Italian bodies. The target was twenty-five cars, enough to make the racers legal. The racer was the point. It was the C-4R: a big white roadster with two blue stripes and a Chrysler Hemi V8 up front. In June 1952, Cunningham took one to the Sarthe and drove it himself. He was forty-five. He stayed in the seat for almost twenty of the twenty-four hours. Bill Spear drove the rest. They finished fourth overall and won their class. The next spring, a C-4R won the Sebring 12 Hours. It was the first all-American car to win an international sports car race.
description: The C-4R was a sports racing car built in 1952 by Briggs Cunningham's small company in West Palm Beach, Florida. It used a 331 cubic inch Chrysler Hemi V8 in a tubular chassis under a light open body. Two roadsters and one coupe were made. The roadsters won their class at Le Mans in 1952 and 1954, and one won the Sebring 12 Hours in 1953. The road-going C-3, bodied by Vignale, existed largely so these racers counted as a manufacturer's cars.
